title: GCSE Physics Diagnostic Assessment
description: Placement test to determine your starting level. Answer each question to the best of your ability — there is no penalty for wrong answers.
instructions: This diagnostic covers all units. Your results will suggest which learning route best fits your current knowledge.

DESDE_CERO.description: Start from foundations — covers all prerequisite skills before diving into physics topics.

STANDARD.description: Standard GCSE preparation — covers all core content with worked examples.

EXCELLENCE.description: Full coverage including advanced and enrichment material for top grades.

FAST_REVIEW.description: Quick revision — focus on key formulas, common mistakes and exam technique.

items.stem: Which of the following is the SI base unit for mass?

options.why_wrong: The gram is 1/1000 of the SI base unit; the kilogram is the base unit.
The newton is the SI unit of force, not mass.
The pound is an imperial unit, not an SI unit.

items.explanation: The kilogram (kg) is the SI base unit for mass. Although it contains the prefix 'kilo', it is defined as the base unit.

items.stem: An object begins at the $2.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ mark and ends at the $9.4\,\mathrm{cm}$ mark of a ruler. What is its length?

options.why_wrong: this is the final ruler position and assumes a zero start.
this adds the two readings instead of subtracting them.
this results from subtracting the decimal parts incorrectly.

items.stem: Twenty complete oscillations take $34.0\,\mathrm{s}$. What is the period?

options.why_wrong: this is the total time for 20 oscillations.
this multiplies total time by the number of oscillations.
this reverses the division and calculates $20/34.0$ with the wrong meaning.

items.stem: A bag of sugar has a mass of 2.0 kg. Calculate its weight near the Earth's surface, taking $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$.

options.why_wrong: this restates the mass value with the wrong unit, treating mass and weight as the same quantity.
this adds $g$ to the mass ($2.0+9.8$) instead of multiplying them.
this rounds $g$ up to 10 N/kg instead of using the correct value of 9.8 N/kg.

items.source_lesson_title: Mass, weight and gravitational field strength

items.stem: An astronaut has a weight of 686 N while standing on Earth, where $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$. What is the astronaut's mass?

options.why_wrong: this treats the newton reading as if it were already a mass given in kilograms.
this multiplies 686 by 9.8 instead of dividing.
this uses $g=10\,\mathrm{N/kg}$ instead of the more accurate value of 9.8 N/kg.

items.source_lesson_title: Mass, weight and gravitational field strength

items.stem: A box is pulled forward with $16\,\mathrm{N}$. Friction acts backward with $6\,\mathrm{N}$. What is the resultant force on the box?

options.why_wrong: adds the two forces instead of subtracting the backward force from the forward one.
has the correct size but the wrong direction; the larger force is forward, so the resultant must be forward.
reports the friction force rather than the resultant of the two forces.

items.explanation: $16-6=10\,\mathrm{N}$ forward, in the direction of the larger force.

items.stem: A sledge moves at a constant speed in a straight line across level snow. Which statement about the forces on it is correct?

options.text: No forces act on the sledge at all.
options.why_wrong: confuses a zero resultant with a complete absence of forces; friction and the pulling force are both still acting.

options.text: There must be a forward resultant force to keep the sledge moving.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes that constant motion itself needs an ongoing forward resultant force.

options.text: The forces on the sledge are balanced, so the resultant force is zero.
All the forces on the sledge must be equal to each other.
options.why_wrong: is not required: the forces only need to combine to a zero resultant, not be individually equal in size.

items.explanation: Constant speed in a straight line means the resultant force is zero: the forces are balanced, not absent.

items.stem: A stretched catapult elastic band, about to launch a stone, mainly stores energy in which store?

options.why_wrong: the band is not yet moving, so it has no meaningful kinetic energy to speak of.
this store depends on height above a reference level, and the band's height has not changed by being stretched.
no chemical bonds are being rearranged by simply stretching the band; stretching changes its shape, not its chemistry.

items.explanation: Stretching a band stores energy in its elastic (strain) store, because of the deformation of its shape.

items.stem: A ball bounces repeatedly on a hard floor, reaching a slightly lower height after each bounce. What happens to the energy that is 'missing' from each successive bounce?

options.why_wrong: energy cannot be destroyed; this ignores conservation of energy entirely.

options.text: It disappears until the ball eventually creates new energy to keep bouncing.
options.why_wrong: energy cannot be created any more than it can be destroyed; the ball's bounces get lower, not sustained by new energy.

options.text: It builds up invisibly inside the ball until it suddenly reappears.
options.why_wrong: there is no mechanism or evidence for energy silently accumulating and later reappearing; it is simply transferred away as the ball bounces.

options.text: It spreads mainly into the internal (thermal) energy of the ball, floor and surrounding air, and into sound.

items.explanation: Each bounce dissipates some energy mainly as internal (thermal) energy and sound, which is why the ball's maximum height falls a little each time, consistent with conservation of energy.

items.stem: Pollen grains suspended in water are watched under a microscope and seen to jitter and change direction constantly. What is the best explanation for this motion?

options.text: The pollen grains are themselves water molecules moving randomly.
options.why_wrong: confuses the large, visible pollen grain with the much smaller, invisible water molecules that actually strike it.

options.text: The pollen grains are pulled by a weak current that changes direction every few seconds.
options.why_wrong: invents an external current with no evidence, when the random collisions explanation already accounts for the motion.

options.text: The pollen grains repel each other and bounce apart.
options.why_wrong: describes an interaction between pollen grains, not the cause of a single grain's own erratic path.

options.text: The pollen grains are struck unevenly, from random directions, by huge numbers of invisible, fast-moving water molecules.

items.explanation: This is the standard particle-model explanation of Brownian motion: an unevenly, randomly bombarded large particle is pushed first one way, then another, by invisible fluid particles.

items.stem: A solid is cooled, but it does not change state. What happens to its particles?

options.text: They vibrate less vigorously about the same fixed positions.

options.why_wrong: goes too far: particles never become perfectly still, even when strongly cooled, as long as the substance remains above absolute zero.

options.text: They move further apart from their fixed positions.
options.why_wrong: describes melting or expansion, not simply cooling a solid that stays solid.

options.text: They change from vibrating to sliding past one another.
options.why_wrong: describes becoming a liquid, which has not happened here.

items.explanation: Cooling reduces the average random kinetic energy of the particles, so a solid's particles vibrate less vigorously about the same fixed positions, without changing state.

items.stem: A cork floats on a water surface as a wave passes underneath it. What happens to the cork over one full wave cycle?

options.text: It moves up and down and returns close to where it started.
It is carried forward along with the wave to a new position.
options.why_wrong: treats the medium as if it travelled with the wave, rather than only oscillating about a fixed position.

options.text: It stays completely still, because only light waves carry energy.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes a water wave carries no energy to the cork; the cork clearly does move, just not along with the wave.

options.text: It moves sideways, in the same direction the wave is travelling.
options.why_wrong: describes longitudinal vibration in a case where the course treats this type of wave as transverse.

items.explanation: A wave transfers energy through a medium while each part of the medium only oscillates about a fixed position; it does not travel along with the wave.

items.stem: On a wave diagram, which pair of measurements correctly identifies amplitude and wavelength?

options.text: Amplitude: vertical distance from a crest to a trough. Wavelength: horizontal distance from one crest to the next.
options.why_wrong: doubles the amplitude by measuring crest-to-trough instead of rest-to-crest.

options.text: Amplitude: vertical distance from rest to a crest. Wavelength: horizontal distance from one crest to the next.
Amplitude: horizontal distance from one crest to the next. Wavelength: vertical distance from rest to a crest.
options.why_wrong: swaps the two definitions, giving amplitude a horizontal measurement and wavelength a vertical one.

options.text: Amplitude and wavelength are the same measurement, read from the same line on the diagram.
options.why_wrong: is exactly the common confusion this lesson addresses: the two quantities are measured on different axes of the diagram.

items.explanation: Amplitude is a vertical measurement from the rest position to a crest; wavelength is a horizontal measurement for one complete repeat, such as crest to crest.

items.stem: A bar magnet's south pole is held facing the south pole of a second bar magnet. What happens?

options.text: They repel, because like poles repel.
They attract, because opposite ends of two different magnets always pull together.
options.why_wrong: treats attraction as a general property of 'two magnets' rather than depending on which poles actually face each other.

options.text: Nothing happens, because both poles are the same type.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes matching poles produce no force at all, rather than a repulsive one.

options.text: They attract, because south poles are weaker than north poles.
options.why_wrong: invents a size difference between pole types that has nothing to do with the like/unlike rule.

items.explanation: S facing S is a like-pole pairing, and like poles repel.

items.stem: Which pair of materials are both magnetic (both would be attracted to a strong magnet)?

options.why_wrong: neither copper nor aluminium is a magnetic material; both would show no attraction.
neither gold nor plastic is magnetic.
aluminium is not magnetic, even though steel is; the pair is not both magnetic.

items.explanation: Steel and nickel are both among the small group of magnetic materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt).

items.stem: What does the nucleon number $A$ of a nuclide actually count?

options.why_wrong: this is what the proton number $Z$ counts, not $A$.

options.text: The number of protons plus the number of neutrons.

options.why_wrong: electrons are not counted by $A$ at all; in a neutral atom their number equals $Z$, not $A$.
this is the neutron number, $N=A-Z$, which is only part of what $A$ counts.

items.explanation: $A$ is defined as protons plus neutrons together; neither alone, and never electrons.

items.stem: A carbon-14 nuclide has proton number $Z=6$. How many neutrons does it contain?

options.why_wrong: repeats the proton number instead of subtracting it from the nucleon number.
repeats the nucleon number $A$ directly, without subtracting $Z$ at all.
adds $Z$ and $A$ together ($6+14$) instead of subtracting.

items.stem: Which of the following lists four planets in the correct order of increasing distance from the Sun?

options.why_wrong: places Earth before Mercury, but Mercury is closer to the Sun than Earth.
swaps Earth and Mars; Earth is closer to the Sun than Mars.
lists the four planets in decreasing distance from the Sun, the reverse of what was asked.

items.explanation: The fixed order from the Sun is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter...; keeping only these four in that order gives Mercury, Earth, Mars, Jupiter.
items.source_lesson_title: The Solar System as an organised system

items.stem: Why is Pluto classified as a dwarf planet rather than one of the eight planets?

options.text: It does not orbit the Sun.
options.why_wrong: is false; Pluto does orbit the Sun directly, so this cannot be the reason for its reclassification.
is false; Pluto is massive enough for its own gravity to make it round, like the eight planets.

options.text: It has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood of other similarly sized bodies.
It is too far from the Sun to be seen clearly.
options.why_wrong: confuses observational difficulty with the actual classification criterion, which has nothing to do with how easily an object can be observed.

items.explanation: Pluto passes the 'orbits the Sun' and 'round' tests but fails the third: it shares the Kuiper belt with many similarly sized bodies, so it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood.
items.source_lesson_title: The Solar System as an organised system
